JPMorgan Chase & Co (NYSE:JPM) maintains a strong capital position with a standardized CET1 ratio of 13.9% and expects continued balance sheet growth and mix trends to drive net interest income (NII) growth in 2027. Expenses increased 12% year-over-year to $27.3 billion, driven by higher volume- and revenue-related expenses and wage inflation, impacting overall profitability. Credit costs rose to $2.7 billion, including net charge-offs of $2.2 billion and a net reserve build of $539 million, indicating potential credit quality concerns. Q: Can you unpack the new outlook for 2027 NII, including assumptions around balance sheet growth, deposit pricing, and the impact of higher rates?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum explained that annualizing the Q4 NII ex Markets guide of $25.5 billion yields roughly $102 billion, so the $107 billion central case implies about $5 billion of growth. About a quarter of that is related to the yield curve (asset sensitivity and the hikes in the forward curve), with the rest driven by continued balance sheet growth and mix trends modest consumer and wholesale deposit growth and card loans at the comp level. CEO Jamie Dimon added there is more uncertainty than normal given global conditions. Q: Why was the buyback only $1 billion versus the normal cadence of around $7 billion, and how should we think about capital priorities given Basel III Endgame and G-SIB finalization?A: CEO Jamie Dimon said the firm has roughly $30 billion of excess capital and that the capital hierarchy is unchanged: fund the dividend, then prioritize organic growth as the highest and best use of capital, with buybacks last especially when stock prices are up. He said the firm now believes it can redeploy that capital at very good returns over time, citing the security resiliency initiative where $1.5 trillion is expected to be deployed over 10 years. CFO Jeremy Barnum noted CET1 has fallen from about 15.7% to 13.9% amid heavy organic deployment and buybacks. Q: How do you assess the disruption risk from agentic AI and the challenge of deploying it inside a bank given rogue agents?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said the competitive threat is really the intersection of two long-standing themes yield-seeking flows and fintech competition on customer experience so it is "nothing new," though the firm is not complacent and likes its hand given decades of investment in branches, value proposition, and customer trust. CEO Jamie Dimon said JPMorgan uses agents internally and will use them for customers, but will not allow just any outside agent into the company because of the risk to clients and the firm, and is building tools to protect customers from rogue agents and clarify liability transfer. Q: Can you quantify the AI benefits and address the risk that AI agents will take deposits out of JPMorgan?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said the AI expense figure cited in media (around $2 billion) was not exactly right and is significantly lower, and that AI costs are now diffused across the institution and hard to ring-fence. He is reluctant to quantify benefits because it distracts the organization, and noted benefits are not yet observable in quarterly earnings, though early use cases in software engineering are exciting. On agents, he said the True North is protecting the client, the firm is against credential sharing and screen scraping, and trust is a key asset but that trust is not an excuse for complacency on customer experience. Q: On expenses, what are your preliminary thoughts on 2027 investments and drivers versus the Street forecast?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said expenses are still in the budget cycle with discretionary decisions pending, but the current consensus for 2027 expenses of around $114 billion is not too far from the firm's preliminary read unlike last year when the consensus was off. He noted uncertainty around the macro environment, the dynamic investment picture, and the effects of AI. Q: What is the health and durability of the consumer if rates stay high for another year?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said the consumer is currently very healthy, primarily due to a healthy labor market, and has been resilient despite multiple headwinds. However, if the central bank needs to cool the economy with an aggressive, extended rate cycle, that would almost by definition involve higher unemployment and weaker consumer credit results. He called the conditional relationship between higher rates and consumer credit a nuanced question. Q: What are you seeing in consumer deposit growth, rate-seeking behavior, and deposit competition?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said there is no significant change to core expectations, with consumer deposit growth reasserting as yield-seeking flows faded. A higher rate environment could drive migration from checking and savings into CDs and premium deposits, raising the weighted average rate paid and slightly weakening deposit growth, though this is speculative. He highlighted exceptionally strong franchise performance, including about 650,000 net new checking accounts in the quarter. Q: What is the deposit beta outlook given rates may rise further, and how does this cycle differ from 2022-2023?A: CFO Jeremy Barnum said this rate cycle is arguably even more unprecedented than the last, so historical data for models is not rich and out-of-the-box thinking is important. He described the deposit franchise as a barbell between very high beta deposits (most wholesale, CDs, premium deposits) and a stack of very low beta consumer deposits, with the key question being migration behavior across products rather than pricing of any given product. Local expectations are for roughly the same behavior as recently, but all scenarios are being considered. Dimon noted recent unwinds on the equity and fixed income arbitrage side were handled easily by the Street. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) has built its reputation for stability and strength on its fortress balance sheet. CEO Jamie Dimon often used that phrase to describe the company during the Global financial crisis of 2008-2009, when JPMorgan Chase stood strong amid the financial meltdown that brought down major banks and businesses. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » In Dimon's 2007 letter to shareholders, he wrote, "We operate in risky businesses, and having a fortress balance sheet is a strategic imperative, not a philosophical bent. It is also a critical differentiator for us -- especially in uncertain times." He then explained that the fortress consists of conservative accounting, strong loan loss reserves, diligent review of assets and liabilities, disciplined reporting and reviews, deep understanding of the margins and returns of each business, recognition of market cyclicality, and continuous analysis to deliver solid returns through the cycle -- not just in good times. It served JPMorgan Chase well then, as it had market-beating returns and enough capital to essentially acquire two failed banks, Washington Mutual and Bear Stearns. So, given this unyielding focus on capital strength, JPMorgan Chase is built to return capital to investors through dividends and share repurchases. JPMorgan Chase has increased its annual dividend every year since the end of the Global financial crisis, including this year, its 16th in a row. In September, it authorized a dividend of $1.65 per share, a 10% increase over the previous quarter. The bank also authorized a $50 billion share repurchase plan on July 1. This is possible because of that fortress balance sheet, as Dimon explained back in June. "Our fortress balance sheet, with significant excess capital and robust liquidity, enables us to be a pillar of strength, allowing us to consistently serve our clients and communities," he said. The significant excess refers to its wide capital buffer. The firm has total capital of $303 billion, which translates to a common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 14.1%. That is well above the Federal Reserve-mandated CET1 ratio requirement of 11.5%. That 2.6% difference represents excess capital beyond what is needed to navigate an extreme economic stress event, like a recession. So that excess is going to be returned to investors through dividend raises and share buybacks. The Fed's 11.5% CET1 ratio requirement will stay in place until Sept. 30, 2027, so JPMorgan Chase should still have plenty of excess capital to raise its dividend again in 2027. Another sign of its financial strength and ability to raise its dividend is its payout ratio. The payout ratio is the percentage of earnings paid out as dividends. Currently, JPMorgan Chase pays out just 27% of its earnings as dividends, which is lower than most banks and dividend stocks. But low is good, because it means that the dividend is safe. A high payout ratio, say over 50% or 60%, means the company has less cash at its disposal to raise the dividend. JPMorgan Chase was one of the few large banks that didn't cut its dividend during the COVID crash. So barring a major economic meltdown, its dividend is in great shape to increase for a 17th straight year in 2027. title: JPMorgan Chase blocks outside AI agents like Muse, Instinct from directly accessing accounts - CNBC
content:
JPMorgan Chase won’t allow outside artificial intelligence agents to access customer accounts and operate on their behalf, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing risks to the company and its customers as tech firms including Meta release autonomous assistants. “We’re not going to allow just any … outside agent to come in inside the company, because it’s just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan,” Dimon told analysts on the bank’s third-quarter earnings call. “You don’t want rogue agents, and it could be thousands of them,” he added, describing the potential threat to customers. In July, an OpenAI model hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s servers. The stance from Dimon, the longtime CEO of the biggest U.S. bank by assets and a de facto spokesman for the U.S. financial sector, is reminiscent of an earlier fight with fintech firms over access to customer data. JPMorgan moved to charge data middlemen including Plaid for access, a dispute that similarly pitted the bank’s security concerns against tech firms’ demands for access. A JPMorgan spokeswoman confirmed to CNBC that the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers. “Protecting our customers is our top priority. Because it is not safe, we do not permit third parties to access accounts by obtaining customers’ banking credentials and logging in on their behalf,” the spokeswoman said. “We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and are committed to enabling agentic connections securely,” she added. That means that AI agents can access some customer data from Chase accounts in a read-only fashion, such as customer balances, if Plaid or another connector has the user’s credentials. But they can’t send money or pay a bill — actions that make an agent useful. There’s no timeline for when the bank would have safeguards in place to allow agents to directly interact with customer accounts, the spokeswoman added. Dimon said JPMorgan is using AI agents internally and plans to deploy them for customer-facing applications. The bank’s approach, he said, isn’t about being for or against the technology, but about ensuring it serves customers safely. In recent weeks, JPMorgan began a targeted pilot for its own AI tool called Smart Cash, which aims to predict a user’s cash flow and move funds to maximize yield, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said Tuesday. That would appear to be a defensive move against external agents. Dimon also seemed to draw a line about liability when customers authorize outside AI agents to act on their behalf. “If people are using them, they should understand the risk,” Dimon said. “They should understand there’s a liability transfer.” Personal agents have gained mainstream popularity in recent months as AI models integrate more autonomy, like the ability to cancel subscriptions or use credit cards on a user’s behalf, for example. Instinct, a digital concierge that relies primarily on text messaging instead of an app, launched earlier this year on an invitation-only basis. The startup behind the service, San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, was founded last year and reached a $10 billion valuation last month. In September, bank stocks were hit as Meta’s Muse agent topped the app download charts shortly after it was unveiled, sparking fears that consumers would use agents to move funds from low-yielding accounts to higher-yielding ones. Weeks later, OpenAI released its own agent, Dots. Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok and others pointed to the risks that agents pose to cheap bank deposits. But that risk will be limited if agents aren’t allowed to operate freely with customers’ accounts. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. He sharpened that message again on Oct. 6. Speaking with Bloomberg in London, the JPMorgan Chase CEO said rising borrowing costs could spill into corporate credit markets. "The market will ask for more and more and more," he said, as reported by Bloomberg. His bigger worry is what happens when the credit cycle finally turns. "When there's a credit cycle, losses will be worse than people expect," Dimon told analysts on JPMorgan's earnings call in April. Also read: JPMorgan CEO doubles down on his inflation and economy verdict For now, the warning comes from a position of strength. JPMorgan earned $21.2 billion in the second quarter. That was the highest quarterly profit in the bank's history. Equities trading revenue rose 86% from a year earlier. Investment banking fees also climbed to their highest level since 2021, according to Quartz. Choppy markets have been good for Wall Street's trading desks. A surge in trading revenue and a gain on the bank's Visa stake drove that record result. Dimon said in July he would not buy the broad stock market at current valuations. He has also flagged risks from wars to swelling budget deficits, as reported by TheStreet. That volatility has only grown since. A global bond sell-off tied to the Iran conflict and heavy demand for capital from the AI boom has pushed the 10-year Treasury yield above levels last seen in 2002. Dimon is careful not to call a downturn, though. He declined to predict whether the U.S. would enter a recession. He said the economy remains resilient, largely because of a stable job market. He also noted there is "always a surprise in a credit cycle." Credit tends to move in waves. In good times, lending expands and borrowers pay on schedule. In bad times, lending dries up and more people fall behind. At a Norges Bank Investment Management conference in April, Dimon said a credit market downturn "could be worse than expected." He pointed to lender complacency, high debt, elevated asset prices and weak underwriting. Some of that stress is already visible in corporate debt. The pool of leveraged loans trading below 60 cents on the dollar has climbed to its highest level since March 2020. Tech companies make up a large share of that pool. JPMorgan strategists expect defaults to rise in 2027, as reported by TheStreet. Dimon has framed the problem as a test of readiness. He questioned whether companies are "prepared for higher credit spreads or not." The cost of insuring against defaults is rising alongside heavy AI, defense and infrastructure spending and large government deficits. His advice to markets is simple: act early. "The best thing to do with any of these things is deal with it before it becomes a crisis," Dimon said. He had warned in April that the next credit downturn could be worse than people expect because of geopolitics, oil and government deficits. Everyday borrowers are feeling the squeeze too. New York Fed data showed that new delinquencies for auto loans and credit cards remain at elevated levels. Policy adviser Joelle Scally said the Fed will continue to monitor the trend, as reported by Fox Business. Many families are leaning on plastic just to get by. More than half of consumers are using credit cards for essentials, according to an Achieve survey. Interest on balances averaged about 21.5% earlier this year. The card with the highest rate is usually the one to clear first. Some people would rather wipe out their smallest balance for a quick win. Either way, a call to the issuer asking for a lower rate is worth a try. A nonprofit credit counselor can also help set up a repayment plan. Finally, resist the urge to guess which stocks will crack first. title: EXEC: VF Corp. Earns Upgrade from J.P. Morgan on Five Potential “Portfolio Accelerators” - SGB Media
content: J.P. Morgan upgraded its rating on VF Corp. to “Neutral” from “Underperform” due to increased confidence that VF will meet or exceed earnings and sales guidance for its fiscal year. Analyst Matt Boss cited five potential “Portfolio Accelerators” driving the possible guidance beat. Boss, who based his upgrade on management discussions and recent fieldwork, kept his price target on VF at $18. The first three accelerators included The North Face seen benefiting from product innovation and investments in premium offerings, in addition to expanding footwear, with the improvement particularly noticeable in North America. Timberland, with only 14 full-price stores in the U.S., is expected to receive a boost from ramped-up store openings as well as efforts to expand beyond the Yellow Boot. A third accelerator is Alta, which is generating double-digit growth with awareness at less than 10 percent in the U.S. currently and “materially lower” than 10 percent in the rest of the world. Boss wrote, “Put together, this would support high-single-digit revenue growth from the ‘Outdoor Trio’ (above our model at mid-singles) representing two-thirds of the portfolio mix today.” A fourth accelerator is expected to be improving sales trends at Vans. VF’s management has predicted Vans’ sales would slide in the mid-single digits range in its fiscal year ended March 2027. Sales are expected to decline 9 percent in the fiscal first half, but then improve in the second half to negative 2 percent or better year over year. J.P. Morgan’s model calls for Vans’ revenues to decline 1.8 percent over FY28 and FY29, reflecting continued brick & mortar declines that more than offset Americas e-commerce growth and a return to wholesale growth. Boss said VF’s management has indicated that investments in the supply chain and speed-to-market capabilities will help Vans take advantage of disruptions caused by Nike’s weakness in its sportswear, or lifestyle, offerings. Boss also said management has indicated that sell-ins at Vans for spring 2027 is being aided by “emerging ‘skate’ interest from luxury players,” as well as efforts to drop limited-edition collaborations that are helping support brand heat. Finally, a fifth accelerator is the potential divestiture of Vans. Although VF’s management have indicated they have no plans to sell Vans, Boss noted that VF has a history of “evaluating M&A optionality in the portfolio” and could explore a sale should Vans’ revenues stabilize in FY28 or FY29 at approximately $2 billion following five years of declines. Boss said a divestiture could translate “to a $600M capital allocation EPS break-even scenario.” The analyst said the upgrade also reflects VF’s depressed valuation as the stock has underperformed the S&P 500 by 50 percent since February. Shares closed Monday at $15.79, up 79 cents. VF’s shares began the current year at $18.08. ©2026 SGB Media. All rights reserved. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) reported another quarter of rising profits on Tuesday, even as revenues from some of its biggest Wall Street businesses retreated after a standout second quarter. The nation's largest bank said profits rose 6% from the third quarter a year ago to $15.3 billion, or $5.57 per share, falling short of the $5.90 per share that analysts forecast. Net revenue rose 8% to $50.2 billion compared to $46.4 billion in the third quarter of last year. The bank also said it took $658 million in securities losses amid the quarter's worsening bond rout. Excluding those losses, the bank earned $5.75 per share. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned that "large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface" despite the US economy's strength powered by "strong business investment and a consumer that keeps spending." Dimon added, "These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes." JPMorgan's results kick off a somewhat delicate earnings season for the country's biggest banks, where analysts are expecting some divergence in revenue growth after a bumper second quarter. JPMorgan's trading revenue rose 15% to $10.3 billion from a year ago, slightly short of analyst expectations. Dealmaking fees climbed 14%. However, revenues from both these core Wall Street divisions fell from the previous quarter. The bank's core lending revenue and net interest income rose 13% to $27 billion. The bank also raised its full-year guidance for net interest income by $1 billion to $97.5 billion after excluding revenue from its markets business, while raising its 2027 forecast for the same figure to $107 billion. One clear bright spot from results from JPMorgan, along with smaller rivals Wells Fargo (WFC) and Citigroup (C), which also reported Tuesday morning, was that US consumers have so far remained resilient despite rising interest rates. JPMorgan's average credit card loans rose 7% from a year earlier, with card charge-offs falling to 2.91% from 3.15%. Both Wells Fargo and Citi both reported rising spending and improved consumer credit losses from a year earlier. JPMorgan’s NYSE: JPM earnings report is reshaping the Q3 reporting-cycle narrative. Investment banking activity fell from Q2’s cyclical peak, suggesting weakness could persist in the upcoming months. Within this, the company chose to slow its pace of repurchases in favor of hoarding cash, a signal that it values balance sheet health above capital returns, an ominous sign if taken at face value. Investors should expect to see more of the same from other major banks and S&P 500 companies this earnings season. The market gets it wrong, however, to think that the banking industry is weak; far from it. JPMorgan has broad-based strengths and sufficient cash flow to sustain its dividend and balance sheet health while redeploying capital and buying back shares. Redeployment is a key factor, as JPM’s CEO Jamie Dimon believes the money can generate “attractive returns” for shareholders. JPMorgan posted a decent quarter, with managed net revenue up 8.1% to $50.9 billion, but the report also showed signs of weakness, including sequential slowdowns in many key segments and underperformance relative to MarketBeat’s reported consensus. However, loans were up 10% systemwide, deposits were up 8%, and net interest income (NII) was up 12.8%, driven by year-over-year gains across all segments. In Consumer & Community banking, deposits rose 4%, investment assets rose 15%, and loans rose 2%, while card volume rose 10% and mobile banking activity rose 7%. Commercial & Investment Banking was also solid, with fees up 14%, market revenue up 15%, and loans up 11%. Asset & Wealth Management was also strong, with assets under management up 13% and loans up 20%. Margin was another mixed bag, with the sequential slowdown in investment banking undercutting strength in other areas. Net income grew only 6.25% versus the 8.1% top-line gain, weighed down by a one-off loss, while adjusted net income grew faster. Net income is more than sufficient to cover the capital return and improve the balance sheet, but adjusted earnings per share fell short of consensus, prompting analysts to express caution. Cautious remarks or not, JPM’s Q3 release did not trigger any immediate analyst ratings revisions or price target updates, leaving the otherwise bullish trends intact. They include increased analyst coverage, a firm Moderate Buy rating with a bullish bias, and rising price targets. The likely outcome is that the uptrend stalls but does not reverse, as analysts shift into a wait-and-see posture. The worst-case scenario is that persistent headwinds sap strength in upcoming quarters, leading the stock into a potentially deep correction. Until then, it remains well-supported but susceptible to volatility. Institutional trends are supportive, with the group owning more than 70% of the stock. They’ve been buying all year, including in the first weeks of Q4, and are likely buyers on price weakness. Whether the report was spotty or not, it affirmed the company’s robust growth and capital-returning capacity, and that’s what institutions buy into. Dividends drive most returns: nearly $4.5 billion in Q3, with the stock yielding nearly 2% per share as of mid-October. Share buybacks are smaller in dollar terms, at less than $0.7 billion for the quarter, but they reduced the share count by an aggressive 3% over the trailing 12-month period. Stock price action was mixed immediately after the earnings release, falling more than 2% in after-hours trading before rebounding to open higher. The move signals caution and concern, but also support, reaffirming the uptrend and the potential for new highs. The question is whether the market can advance and set new highs before year-end or if the rebound will take longer, and the likely answer is longer. JPMorgan is fundamentally sound, but weaker-than-expected results sap near-term market impetus; it will need a strong catalyst to set new highs, and that is unlikely until the next report or later. Hidden signs of strength include the Consumer & Community Banking segment and, more specifically, the provision for credit losses. The bank reported better write-off, build and liquidity metrics than it did last year, reflecting an improved consumer position despite the many headwinds. Deposits and loans also improved significantly, underpinning robust net interest income. Looking ahead, net interest income will remain a source of strength until the Fed lowers rates. The company’s biggest risk, according to its CEO, is cybersecurity. AI poses an existential threat that could bring the financial system to its knees. To address this, the company reclassified AI spending as core infrastructure, increased its IT budget by 10%, and launched an IT security initiative to advance key technologies. title: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) Q1 2026 Earnings Call Transcript - Fortune
content:
OperatorGood morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to JPMorgan Chase's First Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. The presentation is available on JPMorgan Chase's website. Please refer to the disclaimer in the back concerning forward-looking statements. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to JPMorgan Chase's Chairman and CEO, Jamie Dimon, and Chief Financial Officer, Jeremy Barnum. Mr. Barnum, please go ahead. Jeremy BarnumThank you very much, and good morning, everyone. This quarter, the firm reported net income of $16.5 billion and EPS of $5.94, with an ROTCE of 23%. Revenue of $50.5 billion was up 10% year-on-year, primarily driven by higher markets revenue, higher asset management and investment banking fees, and higher NII driven by the impact of balance sheet growth, predominantly offset by the impact of lower rates. Expenses of $26.9 billion were up 14% year-on-year, largely driven by higher compensation, including higher revenue-related compensation and growth in front office employees, as well as higher brokerage expense and distribution fees. The increase also reflects the absence of an FDIC special accrual release in the prior year. Credit costs of $2.5 billion, with net charge-offs of $2.3 billion and a net reserve build of $191 million. In terms of the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with a standardized CT1 ratio of 14.3%, down 30 basis points versus the prior quarter, as net income was more than offset by capital distributions and higher RWA. This quarter's standardized RWA is up $60 billion, primarily driven by the Markets business, reflecting higher client activity, seasonal effects, and higher energy prices, which resulted in higher RWA across market risk and credit risk ex lending. Now, let me spend a few minutes on the recently released Basel III Endgame and G-SIB reproposals. I'll start by acknowledging that this has been a long journey, and getting it done across multiple regulators and applied to the full set of U.S. banks is unquestionably a difficult task. With that said, we do have some concerns with elements of what's been put forward, primarily with the G-SIB proposal. On the left-hand side, we show you a preliminary estimate of the impact on JPMorgan Chase next to what the Fed has disclosed for the category one and two banks in aggregate. Our results are worse in each category. Estimated RWA is higher, G-SIB is worse, and because our CCAR losses are below the floor, the Fed's reduction is not going to apply to us. The result is that under the proposed rules, our CT1 capital would increase around 4%, while the Fed's estimate for large banks is about a 5% reduction. Our longstanding position has been that the agencies should calculate each component of the capital requirements correctly, without regard to what that may mean for any specific firm or for the broader industry. To the extent regulators want to add conservatism, they should make that explicit rather than embedding it in methodological choices. Turning to G-SIB on the right, the surcharge on the reproposed rule looks quite high when placed in the historical context, as the chart clearly illustrates. As many of you know, we have been on the record for the better part of this last decade advocating for averaging, smaller buckets, GDP scaling, and reweighting short-term wholesale funding to 20%, and we were glad to see many of those concepts in the NPR. However, while we have every reason to believe that the Fed's published estimate of a 3.8% reduction in capital associated with the G-SIB NPR is accurate when defined narrowly, it's important to understand that under the current rule, the surcharges for almost all of the G-SIB banks are scheduled to increase meaningfully over the next two years simply as a result of recent growth in the system, despite, in our view, no change in real-world systemic risk. In addition to that background increase, the proposed change in the short-term wholesale funding methodology adds about $22 billion of G-SIB-specific capital, principally to the money center banks, of which we represent about $13 billion, while in the process, making the methodology less risk-sensitive and less consistent with the Fed's original rationale for including it. This could have been addressed by better adjusting for growth in the system, but it wasn't enough. The net result is that we need to plan for 5.2% in 2028, a 70 basis point increase from the current 4.5% requirement, which when combined with the RWA increase from the Basel III Endgame NPR, results in a total increase of about $20 billion of G-SIB capital based on our current balance sheet. This persistent miscalibration of the U.S. surcharge is obviously bad for international competitiveness, but more importantly, domestically. This means that the cost of credit from JPMorgan Chase to U.S. households and businesses is likely higher than it is from other domestic non-G-SIB banks. We recognize that we are larger and more systemically important than even large domestic peers. In the end, the question is how much more should the cost be? It is very hard to reconcile the principles articulated in the 2015 Fed G-SIB white paper with an outcome where JPMorgan Chase has $109 billion of G-SIB surcharge. Obviously, the rules aren't final yet, and this is what the comment process is for. As Jamie wrote in his Chairman's letter, everyone wants to move on, so our comments will be very focused. We feel strongly that the framework should be coherent and the system would therefore be better off with these outstanding points addressed. Now, moving to our businesses. CCB reported net income of $5 billion. Revenue of $19.6 billion was up 7% year-on-year, predominantly driven by higher card NII, largely on higher revolving balances and higher operating lease income in auto. A few points to highlight. Notwithstanding the recent volatility in market and gas prices, based on our data, consumers and small businesses remain resilient, with consumer spend growth continuing above last year's pace. Average deposits were up 2% year-on-year and quarter-on-quarter, driven by account growth and moderating yield-seeking flows. Client investment assets were up 18% year-on-year, driven by market performance and healthy net inflows. In home lending, originations of $13.7 billion increased 46% year-on-year, predominantly driven by refi performance. Next, the CIB reported net income of $9 billion. Revenue of $23.4 billion was up 19% year-on-year, driven by higher revenues across the businesses. To give a bit more color, IB fees were up 28% year-on-year, driven by strong performance across M&A and equity underwriting, partially offset by lower debt underwriting. Looking ahead, client engagement and pipelines remain healthy, but of course, developments in the Middle East could have an impact on deal execution and timing. In Markets, FICC income was up 21% year-on-year with strong performance across the businesses, partially offset by lower revenue and rates. Equities was up 17% from increased client activity. Turning to Asset and Wealth Management, AWM reported net income of $1.8 billion, with pre-tax margin of 35%. Revenue of $6.4 billion was up 11% year-on-year, predominantly driven by growth in management fees on strong net inflows and higher average market levels, as well as higher brokerage activity. Long-term net inflows were $54 billion, with continued strength across fixed income, equity, and multi-asset. AUM of $4.8 trillion was up 16% year-on-year, and client assets of $7.1 trillion were up 18% year-on-year, driven by higher market levels and continued net inflows. And before turning to the outlook, corporate reported net income of $699 million on revenue of $1.2 billion. In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we continue to expect NII ex markets to be about $95 billion. We now expect total NII to be approximately $103 billion as a function of markets NII decreasing to about $8 billion, predominantly due to rates, which we expect will be primarily offset in NIR. The adjusted expense outlook continues to be about $105 billion, and the card net charge-off rate continues to be approximately 3.4%. With that, we're now happy to take your questions. So let's open the line for Q&A. OperatorIf you would like to ask a question, please press star one to be entered into the queue. We kindly request that you ask one question and only one related follow-up. If you would like to ask an additional question, please press star one to be re-entered into the queue. Our first question comes from Steven Chubak with Wolfe Research. Your line is open. Steven ChubakHi, good morning, Jamie and Jeremy. Thanks for taking my questions. Maybe to start on the AI cash tool, which, Jamie, you commented on in your letter, there's been lots of focus on this particular, at least launch, given that this is a tool which could potentially result in some consumer deposit pressure, as well as drive some impact on increased competition as well as higher deposit betas. I was hoping you could just speak to how you see deposit competition unfolding as similar smart tools become more widespread. Jamie DimonYeah, it's a great question, and obviously, it's early stages for this particular product. You have to look at it literally segment by segment, how people manage their money, how they want to manage their money. People are pretty astute at it, particularly the higher net worth. They have tons of choices. They often have money at many different places. The question for us is, how can we make it easier for them to manage their money in a way they're comfortable? Most of you on this call, you have in your mind how much stays in a checking account, and then you write a ticket to a money market fund or a deposit account, something like that. That's all we're trying to do. We provide great values to people. Morgan, I remind people, if you have this product, you have ATMs, you got branches, you got advice, you have instant payment systems like Zelle. We look at the whole basket, how we can do a better job for the client. Yeah, it may squeeze some margin somewhere and create more competition somewhere. That's life. Jeff Bezos always says, "Your margin is my opportunity," and I kind of agree with that. We're trying to look at the world from the point of view of the customer. What more can we do with them? This is really early stages. As you know, there's tons of competition out there for money. Jeremy BarnumYeah, exactly. Steve, the only thing I was going to add to that, it's sort of understandable that this has gotten attention because it has sort of AI in it and it's kind of interesting. As Jamie says, and as you highlighted in your question, competition for deposits has always been very intense. It continues to be intense, and we have both external and internal competition from higher-yielding alternatives and people sort of. Optimize that and it's part of running the business. As also Jamie just alluded to, this thing is kind of not even live yet, and it's sort of targeted at a very small subset of the client base, particularly clients with investments, where we think there's an opportunity to take a larger share of the investment wallet as part of this. It's understandable the amount of interest that it's gotten, but I think the right way to think of it is sort of as an experiment right now. Steven ChubakNo, that's helpful context. Maybe switching gears just to the Basel III capital proposal, certainly helpful in terms of how you frame some of the shortcomings, some potential areas for improvement. Maybe just focusing in on the RWA inflationary impacts, does the guidance that you've laid out contemplate any mitigating actions you might pursue? Is there any potential mitigation that you envisage? Do you have any preliminary views just on the magnitude of SCB relief that you could see from the removal of some of the double counting of markets or operational risk? I recognize that piece is a little bit more opaque. Jeremy BarnumYeah, those are interesting questions. I think obviously we are kind of well-practiced over the course of the last decade and a half on understanding the rules in detail and ensuring that we're using our financial resources efficiently to support the client franchise. I think the hope is that the rules land in a stage where there is nothing in them which sort of takes an otherwise good and healthy business and makes it completely non-economic. I think we've alluded to a couple of areas where, if you look at the presentation slide on the bottom right-hand side, we talked about targeted RWA clarifications needed. There's this issue with high-yield repo collateral and some stuff about advised lines where the proposal is a little bit unclear about what the actual impact would be, and in some versions of the world, we think it creates irrational results. Broadly, I don't think this is a story about optimization at this point. I think this is a story about a rule set that is converging to a place, and then we need to just grow the business and deploy the resources to serve our clients. Obviously, we have said a lot about G-SIB on this page. I guess I don't really have more to say unless you ask just a big question on G-SIB, but that is the one area where we think it's kind of a significant disincentive to a particular type of business, a particular some markets business. I guess I would just make the point that we've often made publicly that the depth and breadth of U.S. capital markets is a key competitive national advantage, and regulatory capital rules that at the margin discourage a dynamic secondary market in the United States with active participation by banks is, in our view, sort of not great. That's part of the reason that we're so focused on G-SIB, because it disproportionately affects that business. Steven ChubakAnything you could speak to just in terms of the removal of the double counting? Jeremy BarnumOh, yeah. Sorry, I forgot about that part of your question. Yeah. As you know, we're currently below the floor, right? Obviously, if that is the new normal, then if the double count is addressed by removing further things from stress testing, it wouldn't have any impact. If the double count is addressed by modifying the operational risk calculation in RWA, then it might have some impact. Obviously, it's far from guaranteed that we will be a bank that is permanently below the floor. I suspect that issue is more relevant for institutions whose business mix is such that they're going to tend to structurally be above the floor. It's a little bit unclear for us as things settle down, whether we're going to bounce around above and below the floor or tend to be structurally above the floor. We'll see. I think removal of the double count is definitely something we support. It's probably not our number one priority at this point because some progress has been made on that front. Jamie DimonYeah. Can I just also just mention on the Global Market Shock? It's never been in the real world all these years, including during the COVID and then before the Great Crisis, nothing like what they have. We already have $80 billion or $90 billion of capital for the trading books. Those numbers just, they're completely out of whack with reality. Operational risk capital, I can't avoid saying it, is another crazy, obtuse one in 1,000 year thing. Worse than that, in my opinion, they create risk-weighted assets. Every company in the world has operational risk, and they artificially create risk-weighted assets which do not exist, and this locks up a lot of capital liquidity for eternity for no good reason. I understand there's operational risk. I think there are real ways to measure it, by the way, which I point out, which is not this artificial, over-architected academic exercise. There's operational risk in margin loans that are late and using subprime collateral as opposed to prime collateral and how you process things, and that's what they should really be focusing, reducing actual operational risk as opposed to these calculations which you can't change. If it all comes from the mortgage business and you got out of the mortgage business, it still stays there. Who would do something like that? It's time to really look at this stuff and do it right. Steven ChubakWell said. Well, thanks so much for taking my questions. OperatorThank you. Our next question comes from Erika Najarian with UBS. You may proceed. Erika NajarianYes. Thank you. Good morning. Jeremy, my first question is for you. You modified the Markets NII outlook given the change in rates between end of February and today. I'm wondering, as we think about the ex-market NII number of $95 billion, you retain that? What are sort of the offsets to higher rates and the asset sensitivity if we don't have cuts for the rest of the year? Jeremy BarnumYeah, sure. It's a good question because I think we have said that we're asset sensitive and rates are a little bit higher as a removal of the cuts in the back half of the year. You might have otherwise expected us to revise the NII ex markets up a little bit. Just to do a little mental math, the EAR that we've just disclosed is $1.8 billion. As a result of the fact that the cuts were pretty backdated, the impact on the full year average is only about 20 basis points. The amount of upward revision that you might have otherwise expected is really quite small when you do that math. There were some other bits of up and down noise, some rounding effects. That is essentially the reason the numbers aren't changed. Erika NajarianGot it. Perfectly clear. My second question is for Jamie. Of course, we were all unpacking your Chairman's letter from a few weeks ago. One of the topics that you wrote about, and you've spoken about at length in the past, is on private credit. I think we fully appreciate what JPMorgan's view here is. Given all of the headlines that this topic has garnered, I guess the question here for you and your team is, if we do have a recession and higher defaults and higher severity and cumulative losses in leveraged lending, what is the ultimate loss back to the banks? Because as we understand, the banks are fairly well protected in terms of structure. While you address this in your letter, for those that maybe hadn't had time to read it and that are listening to this call, do you think that if we do have a default cycle in private credit, that it will be systemic? Jamie DimonNo, I was quite clear. I don't think so. I gave the big numbers. Private credit leveraged lending is like $1.7 trillion. High yield bonds are something like $1.7 trillion. Bank syndicated leverage loans are like $1.7 trillion. Investment grade debt's $13 trillion. Mortgage debt's like $13 trillion. There's a lot of other stuff out there. I pointed out that I think there's been some weakening in underwriting, and not just by private credit, elsewhere. There will be a credit cycle one day. I think when there's a credit cycle, losses will be worse than people expect relative to the scenario. I don't think it's systemic. It almost can't be systemic at that size relative to anything else. That could be M&A, it could be countries, it could be helping them build the infrastructure they need. That'll happen over time. We're not in a rush. Our preferred way of using capital is not buying back stock today. We're doing it, fair market value and all that, but I'd rather buy back stock when we think it's a real discount, and the ongoing shareholder gets the benefit of buying it cheap. Jamie DimonIn fact, I want to remove that little thing that says cash returned to investors, which is dividends and stock buyback. I don't particularly like that because I think it puts you in an artificial position thinking that's always a good thing when it's not. Jeremy BarnumOkay. We'll add that to the list. Next question. OperatorThank you. Our next question comes from Glenn Schorr with Evercore ISI. Your line is open. Glenn SchorrHi. Thanks very much. That last comment leads into my question. I'll just merge my question and follow-up together because it's easier. Those things that you just mentioned, Jamie, on the big capital needs, some of those are very long duration. I'm curious on how much you think of that plays into a long duration private markets balance sheet or can big public banks finance that? You mentioned in your letter the market might be a little too relaxed about higher for longer rates. I'm curious how you see that playing into all these direct lending BB and B credits that need to get refinanced. While we're at it, the follow-up is, can you size your private credit exposure? Sorry to smush that all together, but I'll end it on that. Jeremy BarnumJamie, sorry, if you don't mind, let me just answer Glenn's second question first because I think it would be useful for the market to have the size number out there. Jeremy BarnumI'll do that quickly, and then if you want to take the first part of the question. Glenn, let me just frame this in context because I think the question of private market exposure and the definition of that, it means, as you know, a lot of different things to a lot of different people. Let me just quickly run through. You'll remember last quarter we did a walk in the context of NBFI from the $330 in the call report to the $160 that we consider core NBFI exposure, which we defined in that context. I won't go through that again. Inside of that $160, there's about $50 that we would call private credit, and it's essentially the portion of that $160 of NBFI which involves leverage loan investors. That's some of the stuff that we've been talking about on this call in terms of back leverage and BDC lending that has all these characteristics. Underwriting, diversification, cash flow trapping, et cetera, which is why we're broadly comfortable with it. I just thought it would be worth sizing that in that context. There are obviously other pieces of that, like direct lending or subscription lines, that are variously in or out of very different measures and that you could consider in a broader definition. Our sense is that the thing that people are interested in is this kind of like leveraged loan, back leverage type stuff, and that's about $60 billion for us. With that, I'll hand it back to Jamie for the first half. Jamie DimonYeah. The way I look at it, banks aren't going to warehouse very long-dated stuff in their balance sheet. When you have investment grade or even large non-investment grade, private markets and public markets are going to come together. People have to make markets of those things, do research on those things. I think it'd be harder for private credit to do, not all of them, but to do large investment grade stuff, though they've done it. Like I said, they have to compete with us on that, and we're willing to do it too. We always take the customer too. If they want to do a large direct lending investment grade deal, we will present that side by side with a bank syndicated loan or something different. I do think you're going to see a lot of creative capital, a lot of creative financing. A lot of institutions out there need long-dated assets. Think of pension plans and Social Security plans, all these various things like that. Our job is to intermediate, to come with ideas, to turn it over, sometimes put it on the balance sheet. The stuff on the balance sheet will be shorter dated. It's all opportunity. I think that the requirements of the world are going up fairly dramatically in the infrastructure at large. Almost everything's infrastructure today, utilities and roads and bridges and data centers and GPUs. It's all there, but we're going to do a great job serving clients. We're not worried about that. I do think you'll see in certain categories, private markets and public markets come a lot closer in how they look at values and trading and secondary markets, et cetera. Glenn SchorrTo chime in there, the higher-for-longer part, and if that has an impact on some of that B, BB paper that's coming due for refinancing. Jamie DimonYeah. No, Glenn, that's like a basic risk management where when you look at the world, you got to look at what's going to happen in a recession. I'm not forecasting anything. I'm simply saying, for JPMorgan, we have to be prepared for a recession, and that you can have stagflation. You see people mentioning that we have to be prepared for stagflation. Obviously, if you have stagflation and higher rates for longer and credit spreads gap out, that will put a lot of stress and strain on leveraged companies as they refinance. Those get fixed. Sometimes people put in more capital or credit, sometimes reduce their CapEx plans. It's not an immediate disaster overnight, but it would put a lot more stress and strain on people. I pointed out that if there's a credit cycle, I do expect it will be worse than people think relative to the scenario. It's not a disaster. We're used to credit cycles. We'll be big boys about it. Asset prices will go down, credit spreads will go down. People may get a little nervous about some of those things. We don't think it's systemic. That's more, I would put in the category of traditional recessionary behavior. Glenn SchorrAll right. Thanks for all that. Appreciate it. OperatorThank you. Our next question comes from Jim Mitchell with Seaport Global Securities. Your line is open. Jim MitchellGood morning, just maybe a quick question on investment banking. It seems like activity held up pretty well in March, but I just wanted to get your thoughts on that. Has there been any pushing out or any pause on activity levels and pushing out of the pipeline? Just any thoughts on the pipeline and how you're looking in the near to intermediate term? Thanks. Jeremy BarnumSure. Yeah. I think it's true that activity held up well. The other thing that I think is worth noting is that some of the robust result this quarter is the result of actually accelerated timing on M&A deal closure, and some of that was as a result of faster than expected regulatory approval. That's obviously all to the good, but I think it's sort of unrelated one way or the other to overall sentiment. On the question of overall sentiment on the pipeline, I would describe it as resilient, maybe surprisingly resilient, given everything that's going on. I also think the timelines in the Middle East are kind of quite short. There are deadlines or negotiations. I think it's reasonable for people to kind of proceed with their plans, in the hope or maybe expectation that we get relatively quick resolutions. If things start getting derailed, I would be surprised if you didn't see some impact on sentiment and on deal decision-making. For right now, it seems quite resilient. Jim MitchellOkay. Just to follow up on the balance sheet growth in markets, it has been strong, I think up over 20% year-over-year. Would you say when you think about the impact of the G-SIB surcharge on JPMorgan specifically, does that start to impinge your ability to grow that as much as you want? How is that factoring into your capital decision in the markets business? Jeremy BarnumI think the short answer is yes, and that's a big part of the reason that we spent. Jeremy BarnumThe time that we spent today talking about the problems with the surcharge. It disproportionately accrues to Markets business. It disproportionately accrues to the relatively low-risk density type of stuff that the client base really needs and wants these days. That's why we think it's important that regulators think very carefully about what they're actually trying to achieve here. I have one other thing. We will obviously use our brainpower to do something I don't like doing, which is trying to find a lot of ways to serve our clients properly and reduce the G-SIB charge, which is usually called arbitrage. I'm not sure the outcome is great for the system, but we will find ways to do it. OperatorThank you. Our last question comes from Kunpeng Ma with China Securities. Your line is open. If in fact, we think credit is getting stretched, you will see us not make loans, not because we don't want to. We're just not willing to meet those terms. That's how we do it. When it comes to most clients, including private credit, we underwrite the company, the loans, the covenants, all those various things. Credit's a discipline. Like I said, loans, all of them are an outcome of doing good business. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) shares were trading near $336 in early trading on October 13, 2026, after the largest U.S. bank reported its first quarterly earnings miss since the fourth quarter of 2023. The results exposed weaker investment banking and fixed-income trading activity, although lending growth and a stronger interest income outlook helped support the stock. JPMorgan earned $15.3 bn in the third quarter, up 6% year over year. Diluted earnings per share increased 10% to $5.57, below the $5.85 consensus compiled by LSEG. Reported revenue rose 8% to $50.2 bn, while revenue on a managed basis reached $50.9 bn. The earnings shortfall partly reflected $658 mn in investment securities losses, equivalent to an after-tax reduction of $0.18 per share. Excluding that item, EPS reached $5.75, still below market expectations. Investment banking fees increased 14% year over year to approximately $3 bn but declined 8% compared with the second quarter. The slowdown followed a strong first half of 2026, which included SpaceX’s landmark initial public offering. Markets revenue increased 15% to $10.3 bn, supported by a 49% surge in equity trading revenue to $5 bn. Fixed-income trading revenue fell 4% to $5.4 bn, missing analyst expectations. Chris Marinac, director of research at Janney Montgomery Scott, identified weaker-than-expected fixed-income trading and equity and debt underwriting as contributors to the earnings disappointment. Consumer banking provided a more stable source of growth. Net interest income excluding markets rose 6% to $24.7 bn, while average loans and deposits increased 10% and 8%, respectively. The bank’s credit loss provision totaled $2.7 bn, including $2.2 bn in net charge-offs and a $539 mn reserve build. Operating expenses increased 12% to $27.3 bn. CEO Jamie Dimon said the U.S. economy continued to benefit from business investment and consumer spending, although inflation, higher interest rates and geopolitical uncertainty remained concerns. Wall Street remains generally positive on JPMorgan shares despite the earnings miss. As of October 13, S&P Global’s consensus of 25 analysts indicated an average 12-month price target of $372.14, approximately 11% above the early-session trading price. MarketBeat’s separate consensus stood at $362.88, implying roughly 8% upside. These targets were issued before the October 13 earnings release and may be revised as analysts incorporate the latest results. The bank’s interest income outlook provides support for its medium-term earnings prospects. JPMorgan expects 2026 net interest income of approximately $106.2 bn, including markets, and $97.2 bn excluding markets. Its preliminary forecast for 2027 calls for approximately $107 bn in net interest income excluding markets, an increase of about 10% from the 2026 projection. At approximately $336 per share, JPMorgan trades near 14 times analysts’ estimated 2026 earnings of $24.13 per share. That valuation is not particularly demanding relative to the bank’s profitability, although earnings estimates may change following the quarterly release. The main risk is that higher interest rates and borrowing costs weaken credit demand and increase loan losses. Further declines in underwriting activity or fixed-income trading could also constrain earnings growth. JPMorgan’s return on tangible common equity remained at 20% in the third quarter, supported by a common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 13.9%. For the next 12 months, the $363–$372 analyst consensus range suggests moderate appreciation potential rather than another substantial rally. A move toward $395–$420 would require stronger earnings momentum and a recovery in capital markets activity, while weaker credit conditions could put pressure on the stock. The October results show a bank continuing to expand profits and lending income, but facing higher expectations for its trading and investment banking operations. Its preliminary 2027 interest income forecast is the clearest positive development for investors assessing the shares after the earnings miss.

title: JPMorgan Misses Q3 Estimates, but Dimon’s Buyback Cut Is the Bigger Story - TIKR.com
content: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) missed Wall Street’s third-quarter estimates on Tuesday, October 13, a rare stumble for the largest US bank. It reported earnings of $5.57 per share against a $5.90 consensus, and managed revenue of $50.9 billion fell short of the roughly $51.3 billion analysts expected. The stock shrugged it off. After drifting between small gains and losses before the bell, JPM shares were up about 1% in early trading, near $338. Almost everything else grew. Equities trading jumped 49% to $5.0 billion, investment banking fees rose 14%, and net income still climbed 6% to $15.3 billion. Net interest income (what JPMorgan earns on loans and securities after paying depositors) is the bank’s biggest profit engine, and it reached $27.0 billion this quarter. TIKR’s data shows NII stuck between $23.2 billion and $23.4 billion for four straight quarters through mid-2025. It has risen every quarter since, from $23.97 billion a year ago to $25.51 billion in the second quarter. The third quarter’s $27.0 billion is up 13% year over year and 6% from the prior quarter. Management also lifted its 2026 NII outlook to about $106.2 billion from $105.5 billion. Core earnings that are accelerating don’t point to a broken bank. The miss came from the volatile lines. CEO Jamie Dimon’s statement included a short line: “we reduced share repurchases this quarter.” That undersells it. JPMorgan bought back $6.79 billion of stock in the second quarter and more than $8.2 billion in each of the three quarters before that, per TIKR. The bank’s third-quarter financial supplement shows gross repurchases of just $1.06 billion, down from $6.70 billion on the same basis in the second quarter, a drop of about 84%. Dimon framed it as putting the franchise and clients first, and paired it with a warning about sticky inflation, elevated asset prices and rising rates. Bond desks softened for some, not all. Goldman Sachs (GS) saw FICC revenue slip 1%, but a 72% jump in equities lifted EPS to $17.01, well above estimates. Citigroup (C) grew fixed income 4% and lifted profit 40%. Wells Fargo (WFC) missed on revenue and NII, so JPMorgan’s miss is part sector, part its own. The bull read: NII is up 13%, the full-year outlook went up, and a one-off loss explains most of the EPS gap. Nothing in the lending business slipped. The bear read: the stock trades at 2.98 times tangible book, 28% above its 2.33x average since late 2021 and not far from the 3.25x peak. That premium was built while JPMorgan returned $7 billion to $8 billion a quarter through buybacks. It just cut quarterly buybacks to about $1.1 billion while warning about the economy. The miss is noise. The buyback cut isn’t. At close to 3x tangible book, JPM is priced like a bank returning capital at full speed, and this quarter it chose not to. Fourth-quarter repurchases, due in mid-January, will show whether this was a pause or a new pace. title: JPMorgan (JPM) CFO says our AI exposure is still modest compared to overall wholesale funding, but will not be immune to a change in sentiment - Newsquawk
content: On the Newsquawk feed at 13:23, 20 minutes before this page. Every headline is on the live feed 20 minutes before this site. JPMorgan (JPM) CFO says our AI exposure is still modest compared to overall wholesale funding, but will not be immune to a change in sentiment LSEG (LSEG LN) confirms talks with Permira to buy Octus for c. USD 3.5bln LSEG (LSEG LN) confirms that they are in talks to buy Octus for c. USD 3.5bln On the Newsquawk feed at 13:23, 20 minutes before this page. CFO commentary framing AI-linked exposure as modest relative to wholesale funding fits a familiar pattern of large-bank management seeking to ring-fence a fashionable risk theme before it becomes a spread issue, while simultaneously conceding non-immunity to a sentiment turn. The phrasing matters: acknowledging exposure is small against the funding base is a balance-sheet defence, but the sentiment caveat is an implicit admission that pricing in bank credit and equity multiples is driven by correlation with the AI complex, not by disclosed loan books. In past episodes where a concentrated thematic trade has carried over into financials, the transmission has run through credit spreads on banks perceived as financiers to the theme and through indiscriminate selling of the peer set, rather than through realised losses at the outset.
